plot_extraction.response_text:
Mr. Tymperley, once a comfortably situated gentleman, loses nearly all his money through a disastrous investment recommended by his wealthy friend Mr. Charman. After Charman dies, Tymperley conceals the truth from the widow to avoid blaming her husband and retreats into extreme poverty in Islington, where he begins learning bookbinding to support himself.

When Mrs. Charman unexpectedly finds him, his shame leads him to claim that he lives among the poor by choice as a charitable social worker. His old friends admire his supposed self-sacrifice, while he struggles to maintain the deception and survives on almost nothing.

Mrs. Charman’s daughter, Mrs. Weare, sends him a five-pound cheque to distribute among the needy. Desperately needing clothes and boots, Tymperley begins rationalizing that he might use the money himself, especially since her father caused his ruin. After buying boots with his own scarce funds, however, he recognizes how close poverty has brought him to dishonesty. He entrusts the donation to a clergyman, then writes to Mrs. Weare confessing his financial ruin, his false story, and his near moral failure. He asks her forgiveness and says he hopes his new trade will allow him to live more securely.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is written in a late-Victorian or Edwardian realist mode, combining social observation, psychological analysis, and restrained moral comedy. Its world is sharply class-conscious: clothes, speech, housing, food, education, and manners all function as precise indicators of social position. Material details—the outdated evening suit, candle-end, crossed cheque, repaired boots, sparse breakfast, and eight-by-seven-foot room—give poverty a concrete texture while preserving the protagonist’s shabby-genteel dignity. The settings contrast affluent drawing-room society with cramped Islington lodgings, turning geography and domestic space into expressions of exclusion.

The narration is third-person omniscient, but it gradually narrows around Mr. Tymperley’s consciousness. At first he is viewed externally, almost as a comic social specimen; later the narrator enters his memories, rationalisations, temptations, and dreams. Free indirect discourse frequently blends his thoughts with the narrative voice, especially when he debates whether the cheque might justly be used for himself. Rhetorical questions, exclamations, and elevated phrases such as “Merciful powers!” reproduce the ceremonious drama of his inner life without requiring direct quotation. The narrator remains sympathetic yet detached, exposing both the cruelty of his circumstances and the self-deceptions generated by pride.

The governing tone is compassionate irony. Mr. Tymperley’s friends romanticise his involuntary poverty as heroic social work, while he disguises deprivation as principle: vegetarianism becomes a health doctrine, abstinence a moral testimony, and polluted Islington air acquires “a tonic quality.” This irony is rarely savage. It arises from the discrepancy between appearance and reality, social interpretation and material fact, or dignified language and humiliating necessity. The protagonist is gently comic in his gestures, circumlocutions, and exaggerated courtesy, but the comedy continually shades into pathos. Descriptions such as his “self-obliterating smile” and “lachrymose” politeness condense this mixture of absurdity, timidity, and suffering.

Dialogue is strongly individuated and socially diagnostic. Mrs. Charman speaks in warm, breathless bursts filled with exclamations, interruptions, assumptions, and sentimental conjecture. Mrs. Weare is quieter and more perceptive. Mr. Suggs and the shopkeeper use blunt, non-standard colloquial speech, while Mr. Tymperley speaks with painstaking formality: “Oblige me,” “Forgive me,” and “I beg leave” recur as defensive rituals of gentility. His dialogue is marked by dashes, repetitions, self-corrections, incomplete clauses, and embarrassed euphemism. The contrast between his elaborate politeness and the direct speech of working-class characters dramatizes his social displacement.

The prose uses a broad lexical range. The narrator favours literate, sometimes Latinate diction—“salubrity,” “circumlocution,” “idiosyncrasy,” “initiatory,” “avuncular”—appropriate to an educated social observer and often echoing Tymperley’s own habits of expression. This elevated vocabulary is set against plain accounts of hunger, rent, clothing, and manual work, creating ironic disproportion. Periodic sentences and balanced clauses support reflective commentary, while shorter exclamatory passages heighten moments of temptation or alarm. Parentheses, dashes, semicolons, and interpolated qualifications produce a measured but flexible rhythm.

Characterisation proceeds through an accumulation of revealing physical and behavioural detail. Tymperley’s bowed shoulders, obsolete suit, nervous hands, thin voice, and sidling entrance externalise his diffidence. Objects carry symbolic force without losing realism. His evening clothes represent his remaining claim to gentlemanly identity; the crossed cheque embodies both abundance and practical helplessness; the new boots materialise his half-conscious movement toward misappropriation and then become an accusatory voice in his dream. Respectability is repeatedly shown as something embodied in garments, manners, and access to financial institutions.

The structure depends on delayed disclosure and reversal. It opens with the charitable legend already established around Tymperley, presents him as others see him, and then follows him home before supplying the history that corrects their interpretation. A substantial retrospective section explains his ruin and the accidental lie, after which the cheque episode concentrates the story into a moral crisis. Pacing alternates between scenic dialogue, summarised biography, essay-like social reflection, and close psychological narration. The conclusion resolves the crisis through confession rather than external rescue, preserving the story’s emphasis on conscience and self-respect.

Authorial generalisations broaden the individual case into social criticism. Aphoristic statements such as “Poverty is the great secluder” shift the story briefly toward the social essay, treating Tymperley as representative of educated people stranded between classes. London is imagined as a “wilderness abounding in anchorites,” an image that combines urban realism with moral and religious resonance. The story criticises not overt villainy so much as social blindness: well-meaning affluent people misread distress because convention prevents frank disclosure, while pride makes assistance nearly impossible to request.

The dominant themes are poverty, shame, class identity, isolation, self-deception, and moral endurance. The story is especially interested in the psychological effects of deprivation: altered standards of value, defensive theories, hypersensitivity to humiliation, and the erosion of ethical certainty. Its moral vision is humane but unsentimental. Tymperley’s confession restores integrity, yet it does not erase the structural conditions that produced his lie. The overall style may therefore be described as socially observant realism enriched by urbane irony, finely controlled pathos, psychological intimacy, and an essayistic concern with the hidden humiliations of genteel poverty.

generation.response_text:
### THE TONIC AIR OF ISLINGTON

At the house of Mrs. Charman, in Bryanston Square, there was frequent mention of a certain Mr. Tymperley, whose renunciation of the world had become, during the last few months, a subject of fashionable respect. People spoke of him after dinner, when the servants had removed material evidence of a meal which would have maintained Mr. Tymperley for a fortnight; and ladies, reclining amid shaded lamps and hot-house flowers, wondered whether the poor were grateful for the devotion of such men.

“Not that he has taken orders,” Mrs. Charman would explain, with eager precision. “He is quite independent of any society—quite! He simply lives among them, studies them, helps them in his own way. Such courage! Such self-forgetfulness!”

Her daughter, Mrs. Weare, who had the misfortune to receive most enthusiasms with a look of reflection, once asked what form Mr. Tymperley’s help assumed.

“My dear Agnes, how can I tell? One doesn’t inquire into such things. Money, advice, sympathy—everything, no doubt. I always thought him singular; but Henry understood him. Henry used to say that Tymperley had the most delicate conscience of any man he knew.”

The late Mr. Charman’s opinions had acquired, through death, a finality which they had seldom possessed during his lifetime. He had been an energetic, sanguine person, very rich when money came easily and very persuasive when it was to be placed where more money might be expected. His portrait, over the drawing-room fireplace, showed a broad countenance full of health and commercial benevolence. Beneath it Mrs. Charman distributed her late husband’s judgments as an ecclesiastical widow might have quoted a Father of the Church.

Mr. Tymperley appeared in Bryanston Square on a Wednesday evening in November. He came late, having walked from Islington, and entered the drawing-room with that sidelong hesitation which suggested either excessive courtesy or a wish to escape unobserved. His shoulders, always a little bowed, had sunk beneath an evening coat of irreproachable cleanliness but distressing antiquity. The lapels shone; the cuffs had received some ingenious repair; and the garment, cut for a more expansive period of its owner’s life, now hung about him with funereal amplitude. His shirt-front, though carefully polished, exhibited two minute fractures near the stud. His shoes could be examined only with pain.

“My dear Mr. Tymperley!” cried Mrs. Charman, advancing upon him with both hands. “At last! We had given you up. Agnes, here is our saint from Islington!”

“Madam—pray—” murmured Tymperley, smiling as though desirous of obliterating himself for having caused so much trouble. “The term is altogether—indeed, I must beg—”

“You have walked!”

“The evening is remarkably—remarkably salubrious.”

“In this fog?”

“A tonic quality,” said Mr. Tymperley, glancing toward the curtained windows, behind which the fog pressed upon London like soiled wool. “The northern districts are frequently maligned.”

Mrs. Weare gave him her hand and looked into his face. She was a young widow, not beautiful, but possessed of that quietness which makes nervous people at once grateful and alarmed. She observed the whiteness of his temples, the tremor of his long fingers, and the peculiar lustre of eyes insufficiently fed. Mr. Tymperley, conscious of scrutiny, turned to admire a Japanese cabinet.

There were six other guests. Among them was a baronet who had lately spoken on the Housing Question; a lady who subscribed to three missions; and a young man preparing a book upon the Moral Awakening of the East End. Each found occasion, before the evening ended, to press Mr. Tymperley’s hand.

“You are doing the real work,” declared the baronet.

“The little that falls within my capacity—”

“Don’t depreciate it. We want men on the spot.”

“I am certainly on the spot,” replied Tymperley, with melancholy truth.

At supper he declined soup, fish, and cutlets, accepting a fragment of bread and two olives. Mrs. Charman protested in anguish.

“You eat nothing! Agnes, look at him. This is asceticism. I will not permit it.”

“Merely a system, dear lady. I have found that a restricted diet conduces to mental clearness. Meat, in particular—”

“But you used to be devoted to game!”

“Our convictions ripen.”

He spoke of uric acid, the discipline of appetite, and the lamentable overfeeding of modern society. Happily, no one asked how long he had held these views. The young man who was writing about the East End made a note on his cuff.

When coffee came, Tymperley accepted a cup, though it was his habit to refuse this luxury even when alone with one; and for twenty minutes warmth, sugar, and social recognition combined to produce in him an almost painful animation. He told a story of his old college days. It was not a brilliant story, but Mrs. Charman laughed before the end, and the baronet said, “Excellent!” Mr. Tymperley laughed too, then suddenly remembered the room awaiting him in Islington. His face contracted. Mrs. Weare saw the change.

“You work very late, I suppose?” she asked.

“Sometimes. My neighbours have needs which do not consult the clock.”

“And you never find the life lonely?”

“Lonely?” He repeated the word with an air of examining some obsolete expression. “In such a multitude? My dear Mrs. Weare!”

When he left, Mrs. Charman insisted on calling a cab. He resisted with agitation. The walk was part of his system; he needed air; vehicles made him ill; the extravagance would offend his principles. At length he departed on foot, carrying beneath his coat two sandwiches which Mrs. Weare, without comment, had wrapped in a napkin and placed in his hand.

“Magnificent!” said the baronet when the door closed.

“Heart-rending!” breathed the missionary lady.

Mrs. Weare stood apart. She had noticed that, while her mother urged the cab upon him, Mr. Tymperley’s eyes had rested for one instant on a silver dish containing loose coins for bridge.

He walked rapidly until he had turned the corner; then his pace slackened. One shoe admitted damp at the toe, the other rubbed his heel where a piece of cardboard, inserted that morning, had shifted from its proper place. The fog thickened as he went northward. It gave to shop lights the appearance of submerged moons and transformed every passing figure into a fugitive from some universal disgrace. Mr. Tymperley, holding the sandwiches close beneath his coat, advanced through this appropriate obscurity.

Poverty is the great secluder. Illness may summon sympathy; bereavement has its ritual and even bankruptcy, if sufficiently large, admits of public explanation. But the gradual decline of an educated man through economies, evasions, relinquished acquaintances, and deteriorating linen is a process for which society provides no decent ceremony. He disappears by inches. Friends suppose him occupied, eccentric, altered in his tastes. He, on his part, develops convictions. He discovers that theatres are noisy, dinners injurious, correspondence burdensome, and the outer suburbs full of philosophic charm.

Mr. Tymperley had now been a philosopher for eleven months.

His lodging stood in a street off the Caledonian Road, where houses originally intended for respectable families had undergone repeated subdivision without enlargement. A brass plate on the door announced MRS. SUGGS, APARTMENTS; a card in the basement window offered MANGLES TAKEN IN. The smell of boiled greens, paraffin, and damp plaster met him in the passage.

Mrs. Suggs came from the back room, wiping her hands upon her apron.

“There’s another letter for you,” she said. “And Mr. Suggs says about Saturday—”

“Quite so, Mrs. Suggs. Pray assure him that the matter has not escaped my attention.”

“It escaped it last Saturday.”

“A temporary embarrassment. I hope you will oblige me by exercising for another day or two that patience which has hitherto—”

“Well, patience don’t pay the gas.”

“No. Indisputably not.”

She looked down at his shoes. Mrs. Suggs was neither cruel nor obtuse; but daily commerce with small debts had worn blunt the finer instruments of compassion.

“You’ll catch your death with them things.”

“I have enjoyed excellent health.”

“You look it,” she returned, and disappeared.

His room, on the second floor, measured eight feet by seven, exclusive of a recess containing a washstand. A truckle-bed occupied one wall; against another stood a deal table bearing a bookbinder’s press, some paste, thread, and a heap of damaged volumes. There were two chairs, one unsafe, and a strip of carpet which did not reach any object in the room. Mr. Tymperley lit a candle-end, removed his evening coat with reverence, and hung it upon a nail. From the pocket of his ordinary jacket—greenish black at the seams—he took the sandwiches.

He ate one slowly. The other he placed in a cracked saucer for breakfast.

The letter was from Mrs. Charman.

“My dear, noble friend,” it began.

He closed his eyes.

The letter thanked him for coming, reproached him for walking, praised his “beautiful work,” and begged him to dine again on the following Sunday. There was a postscript: “Agnes is deeply interested, though she says so little. She thinks you must allow us to help.”

Mr. Tymperley sat motionless before the candle. Presently he laughed—a thin, brief sound, no more expressive of amusement than a cough.

Eleven months earlier he had inhabited chambers near St. James’s Street, possessed an income of some eight hundred pounds, and complained that life lacked an object. His father had left him investments of unimpeachable dulness. Mr. Charman, who regarded four per cent as an insult to Providence, awakened him to opportunity.

The undertaking was concerned with timber, minerals, a concession in South America, and rights whose value could be understood only upon a map coloured by the company’s promoters. Mr. Charman had invested largely. More persuasive still, he had declared that he would put in ten times as much if certain negotiations were completed.

“My dear fellow, it is not speculation,” he had said. “Speculation implies uncertainty. This is foresight.”

Tymperley, whose knowledge of commerce was limited to paying bills with unnecessary promptitude, hesitated for three weeks and yielded in twenty minutes. He sold the securities inherited from his father and placed nearly the whole proceeds in the new enterprise. A month later Mr. Charman died suddenly at a railway station. Within another three months the company collapsed amid geographical ambiguities and legal explanations. What remained to Tymperley, after the payment of liabilities which he need not legally have discharged, produced less than twenty pounds a year.

He made no accusation against the dead man. Indeed, as disaster clarified his memory, he recalled qualifications in Charman’s language, warnings half jocularly uttered, and one letter in which risk had been admitted. The recommendation had been reckless; it had not been fraudulent. Mrs. Charman knew nothing. When Tymperley called upon her after the funeral, saw her surrounded by flowers and solicitude, and heard her speak of Henry’s last concern for his friends, confession became impossible.

“How glad I am,” she had said, “that you and he had that business interest together! It comforts me to think his judgment may continue to benefit those he loved.”

Tymperley bowed his head. The movement was interpreted as emotion.

He attempted, at first, to preserve his social existence. He took cheaper chambers, dismissed his servant, sold wine and pictures, and wrote to acquaintances inquiring, with elaborate carelessness, whether they knew of remunerative occupation suited to a man of education. One suggested secretarial work but had already promised the place to a cousin. Another spoke of journalism, as though newspapers maintained a door through which impoverished gentlemen might enter by presenting a Latin quotation. A third advised him to go abroad. All invited him to dinner.

But evening hospitality creates morning obligations. Gloves decay, shirt-fronts require renewal, and the man who has dined must sooner or later entertain, subscribe, travel by cab, or appear in daylight. Invitations became terrors. Tymperley pleaded health, study, engagements, a growing distaste for society. Then, with rent accumulating, he moved to Islington and ceased to write.

Why bookbinding? The choice had in it both practicality and illusion. He loved books; therefore, he reasoned, he could learn to bind them. It did not occur to him that affection for Sophocles provides no natural dexterity with paste, leather, or the paring-knife. Yet he persevered. An old craftsman in Clerkenwell, amused by his speech and touched by his punctuality, allowed him to watch and practise for a few shillings a week.

“You’ll never be quick,” said the man, “but you may turn out tidy.”

Tymperley accepted this estimate as encouragement.

The legend of his philanthropy began by accident.

One rainy afternoon, Mrs. Charman, driving home from a committee meeting, saw him crossing a street near Pentonville Road. His umbrella had collapsed; he carried a parcel of books; his trousers were wet to the knee. She stopped the carriage and called his name.

His first impulse was flight. His second, more gentlemanly and therefore more disastrous, compelled him to approach.

“My dear Mr. Tymperley! What are you doing here? And in this rain! Where are you living?”

He could not name the street. To do so would be to expose the lodging, the arrears, the mangle in the basement. He waved vaguely toward a region of soot-coloured roofs.

“In the neighbourhood.”

“But why? You never told us! Are you visiting someone?”

“I—my time is much occupied among the local population.”

Mrs. Charman’s eyes widened.

“The poor?”

There are moments when a lie is not invented but conferred. The victim has only to lack courage to return it.

“I have had occasion to observe certain conditions—”

“I knew it!” she exclaimed. “I always said you had a vocation. Henry knew it too. You have given up everything!”

“No, no; not everything.”

“Your comfort, your friends, your whole old life! And you never spoke of it!”

He tried to contradict her. He mentioned study, personal motives, an experiment in living. But each embarrassed phrase furnished her enthusiasm with new material. By the time the carriage drove away, Mr. Tymperley had become a voluntary resident among the poor, an independent social investigator, an anonymous benefactor, and possibly a vegetarian apostle of sanitation.

The story spread. Invitations returned, now bearing the additional burden of reverence. And because starvation does not invariably abolish vanity—because, indeed, it may feed upon those fragments of vanity which nothing else can nourish—Tymperley derived at first a mournful pleasure from the mistake. He had failed as an investor, a man of the world, and an applicant for employment; as a saint, he succeeded without effort.

There was food, too, at these revived engagements.

He despised himself after every visit and accepted the next invitation.

Three days after the dinner in Bryanston Square, a letter came from Mrs. Weare. It contained a cheque for five pounds, crossed, and a sheet of paper on which she had written:

“Dear Mr. Tymperley,—Will you do me the kindness of using this for one or two cases in your neighbourhood where a little help may be useful? I should prefer that no name be mentioned. My mother has told me how quietly you work, and I know I may trust your judgment.”

Five pounds.

Mr. Tymperley read the letter standing by his window. Below, a costermonger shouted the merits of bruised apples; rainwater trembled upon a line of washing. The cheque, pale and crisp, seemed to illuminate the room.

Five pounds meant a sovereign for Mrs. Suggs, thus reducing the arrears to a sum which could be discussed without violence; fifteen shillings for boots; perhaps ten for a serviceable pair of trousers purchased second-hand; food—actual dinners—for several weeks; candles without calculation; soap of a quality not destructive to the skin. Five pounds meant, in short, temporary readmission to the human species.

But the cheque was crossed.

This practical impediment first occupied him. He had no banking account. The little branch near his former chambers had closed his account with a politeness more chilling than reproof. To convert the cheque, he must ask some tradesman or acquaintance. Well, the clergyman in the next parish might undertake it. Clearly the money was intended for charitable use.

Charitable use.

He placed the cheque on the table and addressed himself to a volume of sermons which required resewing. His fingers blundered. Twice the needle pierced his thumb.

What, after all, constituted a “case”? Mrs. Weare had left the phrase deliberately broad. “One or two cases in your neighbourhood where a little help may be useful.” He lived in the neighbourhood. Help would be useful. As to number, one was explicitly permitted.

Absurd! Monstrous!

He rose and paced the three available steps between bed and door.

But consider justice. From whom had Mrs. Weare inherited her ample fortune? From Mr. Charman. By whose advice had Tymperley been ruined? Mr. Charman’s. Had he informed the family? No. He had spared them—at what cost! If restitution had been proposed, would five pounds have seemed excessive? It would have been derisory. Morally regarded, the cheque represented not charity but the smallest instalment of a debt.

Yet Mrs. Weare knew nothing of the debt.

Knowledge affects intention, no doubt; but can it affect justice? If a man unknowingly returns one sovereign out of a hundred which he possesses through another’s loss, is the sovereign less truly due because his hand acts under a misapprehension?

Merciful powers! He was constructing a philosophy of theft over a piece of paper worth nothing until endorsed.

Mr. Tymperley folded the cheque and put it into his breast pocket. The mere contact warmed him. He would consult someone—not mentioning names, naturally. Or he would wait. Moral problems often became transparent after a sufficient meal.

That afternoon, at the binder’s workshop, old Mr. Clegg noticed his preoccupation.

“You’re pulling too tight,” he said. “You’ll have the back all crooked.”

“I beg your pardon.”

“Beg the book’s. What’s wrong with you?”

“Nothing. A somewhat delicate question has arisen.”

“Money?”

Tymperley stared.

“It generally is,” said Mr. Clegg.

On his way home he stopped before a bootmaker’s window. Several pairs hung from hooks, thick-soled and practical. A card announced: GENTS’ STRONG WALKING BOOTS, 13/6. He contemplated them with the intensity usually reserved for a masterpiece. His own left foot was wet; the cardboard in the right shoe had curled and now pressed like a blunt instrument against his heel.

The shopkeeper came to the door.

“Want a pair, governor?”

“Not this evening. I was merely—”

“Fourteen bob, them. Card’s wrong.”

“I had supposed thirteen and sixpence.”

“Leather’s up.”

Mr. Tymperley walked on, offended less by the additional sixpence than by the ease with which the man had identified desire beneath contemplation.

At home Mrs. Suggs presented him with half a loaf and a basin of broth.

“From downstairs,” she said. “Girl lodging there didn’t fancy it.”

“You are very good, Mrs. Suggs.”

“Don’t get notions. It was going out.”

“I am obliged none the less.”

She lingered.

“You doing any good with them books?”

“I anticipate shortly receiving remuneration.”

“That means no.”

Mr. Tymperley ate the broth. It contained a scrap of mutton, and he swallowed it before remembering his vegetarian principles.

That night he slept badly. The cheque lay beneath his pillow, an arrangement dictated, he assured himself, by the insecurity of the bedroom door. He dreamed that he entered Mrs. Charman’s drawing-room wearing new boots of enormous size. Every step resounded like a judge’s hammer. The guests turned to look; the boots, detaching themselves from his feet, strode across the carpet and announced, in Mr. Charman’s voice, “Foresight, my dear fellow—not speculation!” Mrs. Weare then asked him to distribute five golden loaves among starving children. He concealed them beneath his coat, but they became stones, dragging him through the floor.

He woke before dawn, trembling.

For half an hour his resolution was absolute. At nine he would take the cheque to the Reverend Mr. Milsom of St. Jude’s, explain the commission, and surrender every penny. At seven he discovered that his shoe had split farther during yesterday’s walk. At eight he learnt that the volume he hoped to finish had been spoiled by his crooked sewing and would bring no payment. At half-past eight Mr. Suggs knocked at the door.

Mr. Suggs was a square, taciturn man, professionally occupied in moving furniture. He entered without removing his cap.

“About the rent.”

“Mr. Suggs, I have already assured your wife—”

“She ain’t me.”

“The distinction, though in other circumstances superfluous, is at present unhappily material. I expect a small sum—”

“When?”

“Within a week. Possibly earlier.”

“You said that last week.”

“And was mistaken. No man regrets the error more sincerely.”

Mr. Suggs looked round the room, perhaps estimating the resale value of the bookbinder’s press.

“You’re a queer sort,” he said. “Talk like a lord and owe nineteen bob.”

The door closed.

Talk like a lord and owe nineteen shillings! There was social criticism, concise and unanswerable.

At ten o’clock Tymperley left the house with the cheque still in his pocket. He intended to go to St. Jude’s. His route led past the bootmaker’s.

“Fourteen shillings,” said the man. “Best you’ll do in that quality.”

“I should require to know that they possess durability.”

“They’ll last you. Your present ones won’t.”

Mr. Tymperley sat down.

He had, in his purse, sixteen shillings and fourpence. Of this, two shillings were due to Mr. Clegg for workshop materials, and the remainder represented his entire available capital. To spend fourteen shillings was madness. To spend Mrs. Weare’s money was dishonesty. But if he bought the boots from his own purse, retaining the cheque untouched, his conscience could make no objection. The rent would remain unpaid; food would become conjectural; yet he would have preserved the distinction upon which moral existence depended.

He tried on the boots. They were heavy, ugly, and magnificent.

“A little capacious at the heel,” he observed.

“Thick socks.”

“I do not commonly wear— That is, the socks at present—”

“Thirteen and six, if you take ’em now.”

“The card price?”

“Need room.”

Mr. Tymperley paid. Three bright coins and sixpence left his hand. The shopkeeper wrapped the old shoes in brown paper.

“You won’t want these.”

“I do not readily discard articles which may retain some—some subsidiary utility.”

“They’re done.”

“Oblige me by including them.”

He emerged in his new boots, taller by half an inch and poorer by nearly all he possessed.

Their solidity at first delighted him. Pavements could no longer penetrate; puddles had lost their menace. Yet with every step came a thud of accusation. He had not stolen the boots—assuredly not. He had used his own money. Still, would he have dared to use that money had five pounds not lain against his heart? The cheque had already corrupted conduct without surrendering a farthing. He had borrowed from temptation.

At St. Jude’s the curate informed him that Mr. Milsom was visiting a sick parishioner.

“May I take a message?”

“The matter is financial,” said Tymperley, and coloured.

The curate, a brisk young man with red wrists, looked interested.

“I can deal with parish relief.”

“No. That is—I am entrusted with a small donation. I prefer to place it personally in Mr. Milsom’s hands.”

“Any particular case?”

“None. The donor requested my judgment.”

The young man’s interest became respect.

“Ah! You’re Mr. Tymperley, aren’t you? Mrs. Charman spoke to Lady Bellhouse about your work.”

So the legend had entered ecclesiastical circles. Tymperley murmured something, bowed, and escaped.

He spent the day in a state of moral fever. Because the cheque remained intact, he imagined at moments that nothing had happened. Because his purse contained two shillings and tenpence, he knew that something had. Hunger would arrive that evening; rent, tomorrow; the purchase of paste, on Monday. Then the cheque would cease to be a theory. He would cash it “temporarily,” intending replacement. He would take ten shillings, then one pound. Accounts would be kept with scrupulous exactness. Later, when his trade prospered, every penny would be restored anonymously.

Thus do men of delicate conscience approach common dishonesty by a private staircase, carpeted with intentions.

At six he returned to his lodging. On the table lay an invitation to Bryanston Square and a note from Mrs. Weare.

“I hope,” she wrote, “you did not think my little commission troublesome. If you happen to hear of some elderly person too proud to ask assistance, I should especially like the money to go in that direction. Pride makes suffering so difficult to discover.”

Tymperley sat down.

The words had not been designed for him. Their fitness was accidental; and precisely because it was accidental, they broke the elaborate machinery of his defence. An elderly person too proud to ask assistance! He saw himself as Mrs. Weare might have seen him had convention not interposed its kindly screen: a hungry, shabby, mendacious gentleman carrying charitable money in his pocket and debating whether Providence had addressed the envelope incorrectly.

He took out the cheque.

For a long while he examined Mrs. Weare’s signature. Then he glanced downward at the new boots. They projected before him with uncompromising respectability. Good boots, strong boots, boots for a man returning to honest work. Why, then, did they seem purchased at the price of his last illusion?

There remained a distinction, and it was a real one. He had bought them with his own money. He clung to this fact, not as an acquittal, but as a handhold above some black descent. Poverty had lowered him far; it had not yet compelled his fingers to endorse the cheque.

He rose, put on his hat, and went again to St. Jude’s.

The Reverend Mr. Milsom received him in a study crowded with pamphlets, boots for distribution, cricket bats, parish reports, and an odour of tobacco. He was a large, untidy man whose abruptness concealed neither sympathy nor fatigue.

“Mrs. Weare?” he said, glancing at the cheque. “Yes, yes. We can use it. Plenty of cases. You wish to select them?”

“I wish to select nothing.”

Mr. Milsom looked up.

“The donor entrusted the choice to you.”

“Under a misapprehension.”

“About the district?”

“About me.”

The clergyman waited. Tymperley’s hand moved nervously along the brim of his hat.

“I have no charitable work. I am not resident here by choice. My presence in this neighbourhood is explained by considerations wholly personal and—pecuniary. Mrs. Weare believes otherwise. I allowed the belief to arise.”

Mr. Milsom leaned back. If he felt surprise, his parish had trained him not to exhibit it cheaply.

“And the cheque?”

“For several hours,” said Tymperley, with increasing rigidity, “I contemplated appropriating it. I discovered arguments—remarkably ingenious arguments. I have not done so. Be good enough to take it before ingenuity revives.”

The clergyman accepted the paper.

“Are you in want?”

“Certainly not.”

Mr. Milsom glanced at the obsolete coat, the hollow cheeks, and the parcel containing dead shoes.

“I beg your pardon,” Tymperley added. “That was untrue also. I am in considerable want.”

“Sit down.”

“I prefer to stand.”

“Have you eaten today?”

“The question—if you will forgive me—is not immediately relevant.”

“It is relevant to most moral questions I meet with.”

Mr. Milsom opened a cupboard and produced bread, cheese, and a bottle of milk. Tymperley protested. The clergyman ignored him.

“You can regard it as payment for carrying the cheque.”

“That would be disproportionate.”

“Then eat without regarding it.”

There are benefactions which degrade because they are offered with ceremony, and others which preserve dignity because they permit no time for its defence. Mr. Tymperley ate. He confessed nothing further, and Mr. Milsom asked no questions until the bread was gone.

“You said there was a misapprehension. You must correct it.”

“I intend to write tonight.”

“Good.”

“The consequences will be unpleasant.”

“Very likely.”

“I shall appear contemptible.”

Mr. Milsom shrugged.

“My dear sir, appearance has had too much attention already.”

This blunt sentence accompanied Tymperley home.

He climbed to his room, lit the last inch of candle, and spread paper upon the table. The composition occupied three hours. Poverty had not impaired his command of circumlocution, and shame repeatedly tempted him toward phrases which explained everything while revealing nothing. He began:

“Dear Mrs. Weare,—Certain inaccuracies, for which circumstances rather than intention may perhaps be held primarily responsible—”

He tore it up.

He tried again:

“My dear Mrs. Weare,—Before acknowledging the trust you have so generously reposed in me, I must beg leave to correct an impression—”

That too was destroyed.

At last, when the candle had begun to gutter, he wrote plainly.

“Dear Mrs. Weare,—I have given your cheque to Mr. Milsom of St. Jude’s, who will use it for people in need. I must tell you that I am not engaged in charitable work and that I came to live in Islington because I lost nearly all my money.

“The loss followed an investment which your father recommended to me. I do not write this in blame. He invested also, and I am convinced that he believed the undertaking sound. After his death I could not tell your mother. When she met me here unexpectedly, I was ashamed to confess my poverty and allowed her to suppose that I lived here by choice. Since then I have repeated the falsehood by not denying it.

“Your cheque put me in a position I had deserved. I urgently needed clothes, rent, and food. For some hours I persuaded myself that I had a right to use part of the money because my loss had arisen through your father’s advice. I did not use it, but I came near enough to doing so that concealment would be another dishonesty.

“I ask you to forgive the deception, and to tell Mrs. Charman whatever you think right. I am learning bookbinding and hope, when I have acquired greater skill, to earn enough for a secure, though modest, living. I shall not again accept hospitality under false pretences.

“Yours faithfully,

“Edmund Tymperley.”

He read the letter twice. It seemed at once brutal and insufficient. It failed to describe the ruined shoes, the broth, Mr. Suggs, the eighteen hours during which five pounds had altered the shape of the universe. But these details, he perceived, were not evidence for the defence. If truth was to restore him, it must not be dressed for an evening visit.

He sealed the envelope and walked out to post it.

The fog had lifted. A cold wind moved along the street, cleansing the air with none of the imaginary tonic qualities to which he had formerly appealed. His new boots struck firmly upon the pavement. At the pillar-box he hesitated only once, then let the letter fall.

There was no immediate transformation. The heavens did not applaud; his rent remained unpaid; breakfast consisted of water and the crust left from Mrs. Suggs’s loaf. In Bryanston Square, meanwhile, a footman would carry the letter upon a silver tray into a warm room. Mrs. Weare would read it; perhaps her face would harden. Mrs. Charman would exclaim, weep, defend Henry, accuse herself, and send for a cab. The legend of Mr. Tymperley’s sacrifice would expire before luncheon.

Yet, returning to the eight-by-seven-foot room, he experienced an unfamiliar spaciousness. The walls had not receded; the cracked basin, unsafe chair, and bookbinder’s press retained their places. What had vanished was the necessity of arranging each object as scenery in a lie.

On the table lay the spoiled volume of sermons. Tymperley sat down, cut the threads, and began patiently to unsew his faulty work.

His fingers were cold and still insufficiently skilled. The task would take hours; payment, if any, would be small. But he bent over it with attention. In the street below, carts began their morning traffic, children shouted, and Mrs. Suggs disputed with the baker. London, that wilderness abounding in anchorites who had not chosen their cells, offered no promise of justice.

Mr. Tymperley asked none.

For that morning, it was enough that the boots upon his feet were honestly his own, and that the next book he bound, however clumsily, need conceal nothing.

The first time the lighthouse spoke, Mara Vale was asleep with her boots on.

She woke to three deep knocks beneath the floorboards.

Not the frantic scratching of rats, nor the soft complaint of old timber shifting in the cold, but three measured blows that seemed to rise through the iron bones of the tower.

Knock.

Knock.

Knock.

Mara sat up in bed. The room was dark except for the pale rotation of the lantern above her. Every twelve seconds, its beam swept past the narrow window and washed the walls in silver.

She listened.

The wind prowled around Blackglass Island. Rain hissed against the panes. Far below, waves struck the cliffs with the sound of doors being slammed in another house.

Then a voice came through the speaking tube beside her bed.

“Keeper.”

Mara stared at the brass mouthpiece.

The tube connected the keeper’s quarters to the lantern room. No one was upstairs.

“Keeper,” the voice repeated.

It was faint, warped by distance and metal, yet unmistakably human.

Mara took the lamp from her bedside table and climbed the spiral stairs. Her knees protested; the damp always found the old injury in her left leg. At the top, she opened the hatch and entered the lantern room.

The great lens revolved in solemn silence. Its prisms caught the flame and broke it into fragments. Beyond the glass, the storm had erased the sea and sky.

No one was there.

Mara checked the gallery, the fuel valves, and the emergency shutter. Everything was as she had left it. She bent over the mouth of the speaking tube.

“Who is this?”

For several seconds, there was only the hollow breath of the tower.

Then the voice said, “The Bellweather will strike the north reef at dawn.”

Mara gripped the brass rim.

The Bellweather was a coastal mail ship. It passed Blackglass Island every Thursday before sunrise, running north toward Fallowport.

“What did you say?”

“The Bellweather will strike the north reef at dawn. Twenty-three aboard. Four will drown.”

The voice sounded neither male nor female. It had a flattened quality, as if it had traveled a great distance or crossed through deep water.

Mara snatched up the signal lever and sent an urgent sequence to the harbor station on the mainland: danger at north reef, warn approaching vessel.

The cable trembled in her hand.

No reply came.

Blackglass stood nine miles offshore, connected to the mainland only by a telegraph wire laid across the seabed. Storms sometimes damaged it, but Mara had tested the line at sunset.

She sent the warning again.

Nothing.

The voice in the tube whispered, “Too late.”

At dawn, the Bellweather struck the north reef.

Mara saw it happen through her telescope. The ship appeared as a darker shape inside the gray morning, its bow rising and falling. It should have passed east of the island, but the storm had pushed it toward the hidden rocks.

Mara fired the red flare.

A moment later, the Bellweather turned. For one hopeful instant, she thought it might clear the reef. Then its hull shuddered. The forward mast pitched down, and black water swallowed the deck.

Mara launched the lighthouse boat alone.

By the time the rescue vessels arrived from Fallowport, she had pulled six people from the sea. The Bellweather’s crew had saved thirteen more.

Four drowned.

For the next three nights, the speaking tube was silent.

Mara considered writing a full account in the lighthouse log, but each time she lifted her pen, she hesitated. She could record wind speed, visibility, sea conditions, and ship movements. Those were facts.

A voice from an empty room belonged to another category.

She wrote only:

October 17. Severe storm before dawn. Bellweather grounded on northern reef. Signal cable failed. Four lives lost.

On the fourth night, the lighthouse spoke again.

“Keeper.”

Mara was awake this time. She sat at the small kitchen table, cleaning salt from the flare pistol.

“What ship?” she asked.

“Not a ship.”

The flame in the oil lamp bent, though no window was open.

“What, then?”

“At noon tomorrow, a boy will fall from the western cliff.”

Mara stood so quickly that her chair toppled.

There were no children on Blackglass Island. There was no one at all except Mara.

“Who is he?”

“Elias Trent. Nine years old.”

She knew the name. Elias was the son of Tomas Trent, a fisherman from Fallowport. The boy had once brought her a jar of blackberry jam when he visited the lighthouse with his father.

“Why will he be here?”

No answer came.

Mara sent a message to the harbor station. This time the reply arrived immediately.

TRENT BOAT SCHEDULED SUPPLY DELIVERY TOMORROW. WILL WARN FATHER.

Mara did not sleep.

At ten the next morning, Tomas Trent’s blue fishing boat approached the eastern landing. Elias stood at the bow in a red coat, waving both arms.

Mara met them on the dock.

“He stays with you,” she told Tomas.

The fisherman frowned. “Morning to you too.”

“Keep him away from the western cliff.”

Tomas glanced toward the lighthouse. “Why?”

“The ground is unstable after the storm.”

It was a reasonable lie, and Tomas accepted it. While he unloaded lamp oil, flour, and mail, Elias remained beside him. Mara watched the boy so closely that he became uneasy.

At eleven forty, a rope snapped.

A barrel rolled down the dock. Tomas lunged after it, slipped, and struck his head against a mooring post. As Mara knelt to examine him, Elias cried out.

“My father’s bleeding!”

“It’s only a cut,” Mara said. “Stay here.”

But the boy panicked. Before she could catch him, he ran up the path toward the lighthouse.

Mara followed.

Her injured leg slowed her. Elias disappeared around the eastern side of the tower. She heard him calling for help, his voice carried and distorted by the wind.

Then she understood. He was trying to reach the signal shed on the western cliff.

Mara forced herself faster.

She found him near the edge. The storm had split the turf, leaving a dark crack across the path. Elias stepped over it just as the ground beneath him collapsed.

Mara caught the back of his red coat.

For a terrible second, the boy hung above the rocks, kicking in empty air. Pain tore through Mara’s leg. She dropped to one knee, dragged him up, and held him until they were both shaking.

At noon, the cliff beneath them fell into the sea.

That night Mara sat beside the speaking tube.

“You were wrong,” she said.

The tower answered at once.

“Yes.”

“Elias didn’t fall.”

“No.”

“Then the things you tell me can be changed.”

A pause.

“Sometimes.”

Mara touched the cool brass.

“What are you?”

The flame above turned. Light swept across her face.

“I am what remains.”

“Of whom?”

But the tower spoke no more.

Winter closed around Blackglass.

The supply boats came less often. Ice formed in the crevices of the cliffs, and the sea became the color of hammered lead. Mara kept the lantern burning through long nights.

The voice warned her of a fire in a warehouse, a fishing boat trapped in fog, and a crack in the lighthouse’s eastern window. Each warning came true, though Mara prevented the worst of them. She began keeping a second log beneath a loose stone in her bedroom.

November 3. Voice predicted fire at Dallin warehouse. Harbor master alerted. One wall damaged, no deaths.

November 19. Voice predicted loss of fishing vessel Mercy Bell. Flare signal redirected her. All safe.

December 2. Voice warned of lantern glass failure. Found fracture before storm.

She developed rules.

The voice never answered a question about anything beyond the event it described. It never spoke more than a day in advance. It never warned her of harmless things. It gave names, numbers, and times with perfect precision.

And with every disaster Mara prevented, the voice became clearer.

By January, it no longer seemed to come from the speaking tube alone. It vibrated through the stairs, whispered in the water pipes, and hummed behind the lantern glass.

Mara wrote to the Coastal Authority requesting an inspection. Two engineers arrived, examined the foundations, tested the tubes, and declared the structure sound.

“Lighthouses make noises,” the older engineer said. “Especially ones this old.”

“Do they predict shipwrecks?” Mara asked.

He laughed until he saw that she was serious.

His report recommended that Keeper Vale be granted leave.

Mara burned it in the stove.

She had served on Blackglass for twelve years, ever since the winter her husband and daughter drowned within sight of the island. Mara had not been keeper then. The former keeper had failed to light the lamp because he was drunk.

The wreck had changed everything.

She took his post the following spring.

People in Fallowport said she had chosen the lighthouse out of grief. Some said revenge. Mara thought both explanations too simple. She had chosen it because ships needed warning, and warnings had to come from somewhere.

On the last night of January, the voice called her to the lantern room.

“Keeper.”

Mara climbed the stairs with her hidden log beneath one arm.

“What happens tomorrow?”

“The lighthouse falls.”

She stopped halfway through the hatch.

The lens turned before her. Beyond it, the stars shone with unusual brightness. The sea was calm.

“When?”

“At six seventeen in the evening.”

“Why?”

“The foundation fails.”

“Is anyone coming to the island?”

“No.”

“Then no one dies.”

The voice seemed to pass around the room in a slow circle.

“You die.”

Mara looked down through the glass floor at the long spiral of stairs below.

“Can it be prevented?”

No answer.

She struck the brass tube with her palm.

“Can it be prevented?”

“Sometimes.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only answer.”

Mara spent the rest of the night inspecting the tower.

At the lowest level, behind shelves of fuel and spare parts, she found a thin line running through the stone wall. Dust trickled from it when the wind rose. She pressed her ear against the crack and heard water.

By sunrise, the line had widened.

Mara telegraphed the mainland.

FOUNDATION FAILURE POSSIBLE. REQUEST IMMEDIATE EVACUATION AND ENGINEERING CREW.

The harbor station answered:

SEA ICE HEAVY. BOAT CAN DEPART AT NOON. ARRIVAL APPROX 1600.

Plenty of time.

Mara packed a small case: clothing, the official log, her private record, and a silver-framed photograph of her husband, Daniel, holding their daughter on his shoulders. In the picture, Rose was seven years old and laughing at something outside the frame.

At eleven, the temperature dropped.

By noon, fog covered the island.

At twelve thirty, the harbor station reported that the rescue boat had struck ice and damaged its propeller. A second vessel was being prepared.

ESTIMATED ARRIVAL 1830.

Twelve minutes too late.

Mara could still use the lighthouse boat, though it was a poor vessel for winter water. She carried her case to the eastern landing.

The boat was gone.

Only a severed rope remained tied to the post.

Mara stared at it, remembering the previous night’s wind. She had heard something strike the cliffs but had not gone outside. The boat might already be miles away.

At two, she climbed to the lantern room.

“If I stay outside the tower, will I live?”

The voice answered, “No.”

“If I go to the signal shed?”

“No.”

“The eastern beach?”

“No.”

“Could I build a raft?”

“No.”

Anger rose in her, hot and sudden.

“Then tell me what to do.”

“I warn. You choose.”

“A warning without escape is cruelty.”

The light revolved.

“I know.”

Something in the voice made Mara’s anger falter.

For the first time, she heard sorrow.

She moved closer to the speaking tube. “Who are you?”

The lighthouse shuddered. A prism in the great lens rang like a glass bell.

Then the voice said, “Mara.”

She stepped back.

It had never spoken her name.

“What are you?”

“I am what remains.”

“Of me?”

“Yes.”

Mara looked at her own reflection in the dark window: gray-streaked hair, lined face, one hand braced against the lens assembly.

“How?”

“When the foundation fails, the lantern falls through the tower. The lens breaks. The light enters the glass, the copper, the stone.”

“That makes no sense.”

“No.”

“And somehow I become you?”

“Not all of you. A pattern. A final thought repeated.”

Mara’s mouth had gone dry. “What final thought?”

The tower was silent so long she feared it would not answer.

Then it whispered, “Warn them.”

Below, a stone cracked with a sound like a pistol shot.

Mara sank onto the iron stool.

Every warning had come from this moment—from a fragment of her own dying mind caught inside the lighthouse, reaching backward through the machinery and the turning light.

“Why warn me about my death if it creates you?” she asked.

“Because you asked.”

“Can I prevent it?”

“Sometimes.”

Mara almost laughed. “You still don’t know.”

“I remember what happened. I do not remember what did not.”

At three fifteen, the telegraph clicked.

Mara hurried down to the communications room.

A message came through in broken bursts.

PASSENGER FERRY NORTH STAR OFF COURSE IN FOG. TWENTY-EIGHT ABOARD. RADIO FAILED. LAST POSITION NEAR BLACKGLASS. ACTIVATE HORN AND MAINTAIN LIGHT.

Mara looked at the clock.

The North Star carried workers and families between Fallowport and the northern villages. If it was near Blackglass, the currents would pull it toward the reef.

She ran outside.

Fog pressed against the tower, thick enough to hide the ground beyond twenty paces. The foghorn stood near the western cliff, connected to the lighthouse by a steam line.

Mara opened the valve.

Nothing happened.

The pressure gauge read zero.

She returned inside and found the pipe ruptured where the foundation had shifted. Repairing it might take hours she did not have.

The telegraph clicked again.

CAN YOU ACTIVATE HORN?

Mara replied:

HORN DISABLED. LIGHT OPERATIONAL.

The answer came:

NORTH STAR REPORTS LIGHT NOT VISIBLE.

Of course it was not visible. The lantern had been designed for clear distances, its beam thrown low across the water. In dense fog, much of the light scattered uselessly overhead.

Mara climbed to the lantern room and opened the ventilation panels. Cold vapor curled inside.

“Will the North Star strike the reef?” she asked.

“Yes,” said the tower.

“How many die?”

“Twenty-eight.”

“All of them?”

“Yes.”

The clock read four ten.

“Unless I change it.”

“Unless you change it.”

Mara examined the lens. It weighed nearly three tons and floated on a circular bed of mercury. The rotating assembly could not be aimed downward without dismantling its supports.

But beneath the main mechanism was an emergency tilt gear, installed decades earlier and never used. It allowed engineers to angle the lamp during maintenance.

She found the iron crank in a cabinet. The wheel resisted her. Rust flaked beneath her gloves.

Mara pulled harder.

The mechanism groaned. The beam dipped by half a degree.

Below her, the tower trembled.

“Stop,” said the voice.

Mara froze.

“You told me to warn them.”

“The lens supports the central column. Tilting it worsens the fracture.”

“If I lower the beam, will the ferry see it?”

“Yes.”

“Will they survive?”

“Yes.”

“And the tower?”

“Falls sooner.”

“How much sooner?”

“Unknown.”

Mara looked at the clock.

Four twenty-two.

The rescue vessel would not arrive until half past six. The predicted collapse was at six seventeen. Earlier could mean five minutes or two hours.

She turned the crank.

Metal screamed beneath the floor. The beam lowered through the fog, changing from a pale halo to a bright horizontal wound.

Mara descended to the telegraph.

LIGHT LOWERED. ASK NORTH STAR TO CONFIRM.

Minutes passed.

The crack in the wall widened. Seawater seeped through and spread across the floor.

At four thirty-eight, the reply came.

NORTH STAR HAS VISUAL. ALTERING COURSE EAST.

Mara sat down, weak with relief.

Then another message followed.

REQUEST MAINTAIN LIGHT UNTIL CLEAR OF REEF. ESTIMATED FORTY MINUTES.

The tower shook again.

Mara climbed back to the lantern room. Several bolts had risen from the floor. The lens tilted toward the sea, rotating unevenly. Each turn sent a pulse through the central column.

“Will it last forty minutes?” she asked.

“I do not know.”

“Did it last before?”

“There was no before.”

For the first time, Mara understood that the voice was changing too. Every choice she made carried her beyond its memory. The future speaking to her was becoming a future that might never exist.

At five, part of the western gallery broke away and vanished into the fog.

At five twelve, the rotation mechanism jammed. The beam stopped with its light pointed north, toward the reef.

It was exactly where Mara needed it.

At five nineteen, the telegraph cable failed.

Mara returned to the lantern room and watched the white beam narrow into the fog. Somewhere beyond it, twenty-eight people were following the light to safety.

The floor leaned beneath her feet.

“You should go down,” said the voice.

“Where?”

“The eastern doorway. When the tower falls, run toward the cliff path.”

“You said I die outside.”

“That was before.”

Mara smiled despite herself. “You’re learning uncertainty.”

“I am losing memory.”

The voice had weakened. It no longer filled the room. It came softly through the tube, as it had on the first night.

“Are you afraid?” Mara asked.

“Yes.”

“So am I.”

At five thirty-one, she saw a shape in the fog.

The North Star emerged broadside to the island, so close that Mara could distinguish people crowded along its upper deck. The ferry’s horn bellowed. Passengers waved coats, scarves, and bare hands.

The vessel had cleared the reef.

Mara raised one arm, though she knew they could not see her behind the glare.

The ferry turned east and disappeared.

“You warned them,” said the tower.

“We did.”

The lens gave a violent lurch.

Mara hurried down the stairs. She had nearly reached the bottom when the upper column snapped.

The sound was enormous.

Glass burst overhead. The iron staircase twisted. Mara threw herself through the eastern doorway as the lantern plunged through the tower’s center.

The ground rolled beneath her. She ran.

Her injured leg buckled halfway to the path, and she fell. Behind her, Blackglass Lighthouse folded inward. Walls that had endured ninety winters collapsed in a cloud of stone and copper dust.

Something struck the ground beside Mara—a curved shard from the great lens. It flashed once, holding a fragment of light, then went dark.

The cliff cracked.

Mara crawled forward.

The earth behind her dropped into the sea, carrying the ruins of the tower with it. A wave rose against the rocks and washed across the path. Icy water closed over Mara’s legs, pulled her backward, and then withdrew.

She clung to the roots of a thornbush.

When the ground became still, she rolled onto her back.

The fog had begun to lift. Above her, the evening sky was streaked with red. The island seemed impossibly empty without the lighthouse.

Mara checked her watch.

Six seventeen.

From the eastern water came the chug of an engine.

The rescue vessel appeared through the thinning mist, its deck crowded with sailors. They lowered a boat and rowed toward shore.

As they carried Mara aboard, she kept one hand closed around the glass shard.

Months later, a smaller iron lighthouse was built on Blackglass Island. It had an electric lamp, a radio, and foundations sunk deep into the rock. The Coastal Authority offered Mara a pension.

She refused it.

On her first night back, she climbed the new tower and placed the shard from the old lens beside the window.

At midnight, the lamp rotated north.

The glass caught the beam, and for an instant Mara heard a faint sound like a voice at the far end of a long brass tube.

“Keeper.”

Mara waited.

The light turned again.

No warning came.

Outside, the sea was calm, and every ship reached home.
